findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in AC5 the concrete source and path of the 40+ consecutive Jira revisions needed for the packed-cost measurement (e.g., a checked-in replay fixture, a `make generate-corpus` target, or an explicit note that the operator attests this from session_log 1cb6-d553-6565-49b4 and marks the AC `[operator-attested]`).
evidence: 'rebuild N>=40 consecutive revisions in a clean repo, repack --window=250 --depth=50, (pack_N-pack_1)/(N-1)' — no source for the 40 revisions
'session_log 1cb6-d553-6565-49b4 (measured facts; do not re-derive)' — log referenced but corpus access not described
'Tier: repo-level measurement' — no file path, no command to obtain the corpus
findings.finding: AC5's measurement protocol requires rebuilding N>=40 consecutive real Jira revisions in a 'clean repo', but the plan never states where this revision corpus lives — no fixture path, no data-export procedure, no reference to a checked-in replay set. The session_log citation provides evidence the measurement was done once, not a reachable corpus for the executor.
scenarios: An executing agent completes all code changes and unit/integration tests but cannot run AC5 because there is no stated corpus of 40+ Jira revisions to replay, blocking the sign-off criterion.

If the corpus is an internal fixture the agent is expected to reuse from the session log, its path must be stated; if it must be regenerated from a live Jira environment, the procedure must be stated.
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) add a fixture path such as `tests/fixtures/corpus/bindings_revisions/` containing the 40 bindings.json snapshots and reference it in AC5, or (b) prefix AC5 with `[operator-attested]` and record the session_log attestation on the ticket, since the measurement evidence already exists in session_log 1cb6-d553-6565-49b4 and re-running it requires production data.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC (unit or integration) asserting that when the baseline value changes between calls to `set_baseline`, the updated value IS persisted — validating the 'guard lets writes through' branch of the new conditional.
evidence: AC1 states: 'Two consecutive reconciler passes over unchanged Jira state produce a byte-identical bindings.json and create no commit' — this only exercises the skip-write branch.
No AC names a scenario where Jira state has changed and verifies the file IS updated post-guard.
The 'Approach' section says 'return early if equal' but never asks for a test that verifies the non-early-return path writes correctly.
findings.finding: The plan names no test asserting that when the baseline value DOES change, the write-when-changed guard lets the write through (the 'changed → write' branch). All stated ACs can be satisfied by a trivially broken 'never write' implementation: AC1 passes (no commit on unchanged state), AC2 passes (stamp absent), AC3 passes (round-trip unit test is independent of the guard branch), AC4 passes (stamp-assertion removed). The guard's positive branch is untested by any named criterion.
scenarios: A developer implements the guard as `return` unconditionally (or with an inverted condition), satisfying every stated AC while breaking the feature entirely for real Jira edits.
Once real Jira edits arrive (acknowledged in the plan: 'correct behaviour once real Jira edits arrive'), the guard silently suppresses all writes because the positive branch was never validated.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to AC1 or as a new AC: 'A reconciler pass that observes a changed baseline field produces an updated bindings.json (file bytes differ from the previous version and a commit is created).' A unit test on `set_baseline` directly is also acceptable: call with value A, then call with value B, assert the stored baseline reflects B.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).

findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a one-time migration step (or a lazy cleanup in `set_baseline`) that drops `baseline_advanced_at` from entries being read/written, so existing stored entries shed the field rather than retaining it indefinitely.
evidence: Plan: 'never write `baseline_advanced_at`' (Approach section)
Plan: 'grep -rn baseline_advanced_at src/ returns nothing; the stamp is absent from every entry written by set_baseline' — the AC guards future writes but says nothing about existing entries
Plan: 'return early if equal' — early return means the existing entry (which may have baseline_advanced_at) is never touched, so the field persists in place
The AC2 grep checks src/ (source code), not bindings.json (data), so passing AC2 is consistent with the field living forever in stored data
findings.finding: The plan deletes `baseline_advanced_at` from the write path but provides no migration or cleanup for entries already written to `bindings.json` that carry the field. Because `set_baseline` now returns early when the baseline is unchanged, those existing entries will retain the dead field indefinitely — it is never overwritten and never removed. The T9 RETIRE checklist item requires a cleanup path; none is specified.
findings.location: ## Approach — 'never write `baseline_advanced_at`'; ## Acceptance Criteria — AC2 ('grep -rn baseline_advanced_at src/ returns nothing')
scenarios: A repo that has run the old reconciler: after deploying this change, all existing bindings entries silently retain `baseline_advanced_at` in `bindings.json` indefinitely; any tooling or future reader that grep-searches the data file for the field will find it, and the pack-size benefit is reduced for existing entries that never undergo a baseline change.
findings.suggested_fix: In `set_baseline`, after the early-return guard, unconditionally call `entry.pop('baseline_advanced_at', None)` before saving — this piggybacks cleanup on the next natural write without requiring a separate migration sweep. Alternatively, add a one-off migration in `binding_store.py`'s load path that strips the field on first read.

findings.finding: The plan removes `baseline_advanced_at` from the `bindings.json` schema — a serialized data shape change — and acknowledges no in-src/ readers, but provides no rollback/back-out plan or expand-contract sequencing. findings.location: Approach section; Acceptance Criteria (no AC covers rollback)
scenarios: A downstream script or monitoring tool reads `baseline_advanced_at` from `bindings.json`; after deploy the field vanishes with no warning and no documented rollback procedure.
A deploy is rolled back: old code resumes writing the field, but any entries written during the window lack it, producing inconsistent data with no documented recovery path.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'Rollback' subsection: note that (a) old code will simply re-stamp the field on next write, so a code revert is safe; (b) `bindings.json` entries lacking the field are harmless to prior code because the field was only read in a test assertion; (c) if any external tooling reads the field, enumerate it or assert its absence.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the comparison contract precisely: the guard should compare `new_baseline == entry.get('baseline', {})` where `new_baseline` is built with the same `{k: fields.get(k) for k in _BASELINE_FIELDS if k in fields}` expression, so a snapshot field that disappears (causing it to be absent from the new filtered dict but present in the old stored baseline) correctly triggers a write rather than silently retaining a stale value.
evidence: binding_store.py:463: entry['baseline'] = {k: fields.get(k) for k in _BASELINE_FIELDS if k in fields} — uses 'if k in fields', so absent keys are DROPPED from the new baseline
If existing baseline = {'summary': 'S', 'status': 'Open'} and new fields has no 'status', new filtered = {'summary': 'S'}, and dict equality fails — a write happens even though no Jira value changed
The plan does not address this asymmetry
findings.finding: The write-when-changed equality comparison is under-specified for the edge case where the existing stored baseline contains a key that the incoming `fields` dict omits. The plan says 'compare to the existing one, return early if equal' without specifying that the comparison must be between the newly-built filtered dict and `entry.get('baseline')` using the same `if k in fields` semantics. If a snapshot field disappears (e.g. a Jira field becomes absent), the new filtered dict will lack that key while the old baseline retains it, producing a spurious mismatch and defeating the guard.
findings.location: Approach section — 'build the filtered baseline, compare to the existing one, return early if equal'
scenarios: A Jira snapshot entry temporarily omits a field (e.g. assignee is null and not serialized by the Jira API); every subsequent pass rewrites the baseline for that binding despite no true change
